title: Comenzó temporada de turismo antártico 2025-2026: Magallanes abre las puertas al continente blanco
content: The Antarctic tourism season 2025-2026 officially began with the arrival of the Magellan Explorer and a ceremony organized by Antarctic21, the Magallanes Tourism Chamber, and the Austral Port Enterprise (EPAustral). From now until March, thousands of international travelers will depart from the Magallanes Region to experience one of the planet’s most exclusive adventures: exploring Antarctica. This season includes 164 cruise calls in the region, with 86 dedicated to the Antarctic route, departing from Punta Arenas, Ushuaia, and Puerto Williams. Authorities project a nearly 10% annual growth in this sector, driven by global interest in Antarctica and sustained recovery post-pandemic. Chile, particularly the Magallanes Region, plays a strategic role: Punta Arenas hosts most air and maritime operations, while Puerto Williams and Puerto Natales are emerging as new embarkation points. To meet demand, EPAustral is advancing infrastructure projects, including the expansion of the Arturo Prat Terminal in Punta Arenas, a new pier in Puerto Williams in partnership with the Navy, and a modern passenger terminal supported by the Regional Government. These upgrades aim to enhance service standards and diversify port offerings. Antarctic tourism has seen sustained growth: after a near-total halt in 2020, the 2023-2024 season reached a record over 125,000 international visitors, confirming Antarctica’s status as a global aspirational destination. Travelers come from over 50 nationalities seeking unique experiences such as navigating glaciers, observing penguin colonies, spotting whales, and visiting scientific bases. Most trips are luxury expeditions with strong educational and environmental components. Expeditions are carefully regulated, focusing on the Antarctic Peninsula and nearby islands—regions with the highest accessibility and biodiversity—while more exclusive long-distance or luxury trips reach remote areas. The International Association of Antarctic Tour Operators (IAATO) enforces strict environmental standards, including passenger limits at landings, biosecurity protocols, and requirements for cleaner fuels. The central challenge remains balancing tourism growth with the preservation of Antarctica’s fragile ecosystem, which holds the planet’s largest freshwater reserve and plays a critical role in global climate stability.

title: ¡En un año! Rompió Antártida récord de deshielo
content: According to preliminary data from the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, Antarctica reached its third-lowest winter ice extent in nearly half a century of satellite monitoring in 2025. The maximum ice extent was recorded on September 17, 2025, at nearly 18 million square kilometers, a level likely influenced by the growing impact of climate change on the Southern Pole. This figure ranks as the third-lowest, behind the record lows of 2023 and 2024, which were the lowest in 47 years of measurements. The past three years have consistently fallen well below historical averages. Although floating sea ice does not directly raise sea levels when it melts, its retreat replaces highly reflective white surfaces with darker blue water, which absorbs solar energy instead of reflecting it back into space. Additionally, sea ice acts as a stabilizing buffer, preventing the Antarctic ice sheet from entering the ocean and amplifying sea level rise, while also reducing wave impact on coasts and mitigating wind effects on the ocean.

title: Antarctique: des changements "abrupts" en cours, alertent des chercheurs
content: Scientists have warned of 'abrupt' changes in the Antarctic environment, which could have catastrophic consequences for the world, according to a study published in Nature. The researchers, mostly based in Australia, highlight 'the emergence of evidence of rapid changes' in the Antarctic environment: retreat of the ice shelf, slowing of an ocean current, melting of the glacier, and threats to species such as the emperor penguin. 'Antarctica is showing worrying signs of change from the point of view of ice, ocean, and ecosystems. Some of these abrupt changes will be difficult to stop and will have effects for future generations,' summarizes Nerilie Abram, researcher at the Australian National University and lead author of the study. The scientists have been warning for years about the risks posed by human-caused climate change for Antarctica and its potentially catastrophic consequences, such as the rise in sea levels caused by ice melting. However, the study also shows how these changes are 'interconnected' with each other and can also exacerbate climate change, notes Nerilie Abram. The retreat of the ice shelf, for example, reduces its ability to reflect solar energy (albedo effect), thus exacerbating warming. The British Antarctic Survey (BAS) has also shown in a study published in June that emperor penguin colonies are declining faster than expected due to the retreat of this ice shelf. The slowing of the Antarctic ocean current and the melting of the glaciers also reinforce each other, a vicious circle that scientists call a feedback loop. These phenomena encourage long-term warming or sea level rise. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet has already been identified by scientists as exposed to the risk of an irreversible collapse due to rising temperatures. Unlike sea ice, its melting increases sea levels, a phenomenon that could last for centuries and persist even if the climate stabilizes. This area of Antarctica contains enough frozen water to raise global sea levels by about six meters. Half of this mass, equivalent to about three meters, is at risk of a next irreversible collapse. In conclusion, the authors estimate that 'the only certain way to reduce the risk of abrupt changes in the Antarctic environment is to proceed with rapid and deep reductions in CO2 emissions this decade' and limit warming to as close to 1.5°C as possible, the most ambitious limit of the Paris Agreement.

title: Atlas Ocean Voyages Highlights 2025 Holiday Expeditions in Antarctica
content:
Atlas Ocean Voyages has announced a series of holiday expeditions to Antarctica for 2025, aimed at travelers seeking penguins and icy landscapes. The company offers three distinct itineraries that depart from Ushuaia, Argentina, and include a passage through the Drake Passage before reaching the Antarctic continent.

1. **Exploring the Last Continent** – Two 11‑night trips begin on 18 November 2025 and 20 November 2025.  The voyage departs Ushuaia at 6 pm, takes roughly three days to cross the Drake Passage, and then spends six days exploring Antarctica with activities such as shore landings and zodiac safaris.  The cheapest option is a 183‑square‑foot Adventure Oceanview Stateroom on the 20 November trip for $10,854.

2. **Crossing the Antarctic Circle** – Two 11‑night trips start on 17 December 2025 and 28 December 2025.  The schedule mirrors the first series, with a similar passage and six‑day Antarctic exploration.  The lowest‑priced cabin is a 270‑square‑foot Horizon Stateroom on the 28 December trip for $15,444.

3. **Antarctic Discovery** – Three 9‑night trips depart on 18 December 2025, 27 December 2025, and 28 December 2025.  These shorter voyages allocate only four days to Antarctic exploration, with the remaining time spent traveling to and from the continent.  The most affordable option is a 183‑square‑foot Adventure Oceanview Stateroom on the 18 December trip for $10,394.

James A. Rodriguez, president and CEO of Atlas Ocean Voyages, said in a press release that "Celebrating the holidays in Antarctica allows guests to create unforgettable memories that transcend the ordinary." The trips are marketed as a unique way to celebrate the holiday season, with the December 28th departures offering a New Year’s celebration in Antarctica.

The article, originally reported by TravelHost on 30 August 2025, provides detailed pricing and itinerary information for each expedition, emphasizing the company’s focus on adventure and comfort for holiday travelers.

title: Antártida rompe récords de deshielo en pleno invierno | Periódico Zócalo | Noticias de Saltillo, Torreón,  Piedras Negras, Monclova, Acuña
content: The Antarctic sea ice extent reached its third-lowest winter maximum in nearly 50 years of satellite monitoring, according to researchers, highlighting the growing influence of climate change on the Southern Hemisphere's polar region. The ice reached its peak on September 17, 2025, covering approximately 18 million square kilometers—according to preliminary data from the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado Boulder. This marks the third-lowest level, behind the record lows of 2023 and 2024, which were the lowest in 47 years of measurements. The past three years have consistently fallen well below historical averages. Senior scientist Ted Scambos from the University of Colorado Boulder stated that prior to 2016, Antarctic sea ice showed a slight, erratic increase over time. However, 'the global ocean warming is now mixing with waters near Antarctica,' indicating that climate change has finally reached the planet’s southernmost frozen seas. Although floating sea ice does not directly raise sea levels when it melts, its retreat replaces reflective white surfaces with dark blue water, which absorbs solar energy instead of reflecting it back into space. This contributes to further warming. Sea ice also acts as a stabilizing buffer, preventing the Antarctic land ice from entering the ocean and amplifying sea level rise, reducing wave impact on coasts, and dampening wind effects on the ocean. On the other hand, it may lead to increased snowfall on the continent, as warmer, moister air near the coast brings more moisture to storms, potentially offsetting sea level rise through greater accumulation. The Antarctic ice sheet holds enough land-based ice to raise global sea levels significantly, though such a catastrophic outcome would likely unfold over centuries. The oceans absorb 90% of the heat generated by human-caused global warming.

title: 仅次于前两年 今年南极海冰范围冬季峰值为第三低
content: According to the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), the Antarctic sea ice extent reached its annual peak on September 17, 2025, at 17.81 million square kilometers, marking the third-lowest peak since satellite records began in 1979. This level is slightly above the 2023 and 2024 peaks, with the lowest recorded peak occurring in 2023 at 16.96 million square kilometers. The NSIDC notes that Antarctic sea ice extent had remained relatively stable or even slightly increased for decades, but since August 2016, a declining trend has emerged in most years. Researchers suggest this trend is linked to warming near the ocean surface, and reduced sea ice diminishes Antarctica’s ability to reflect sunlight, potentially accelerating global warming. The data was based on preliminary satellite analysis.

title: Dotación 2025-2026 iniciará misión en la Base Antártica del Ejército
content: The 78th Antarctic Deployment, consisting of 22 personnel from various units of the Chilean Army, was officially bid farewell in a ceremony at the Army's General Headquarters. The event was presided over by Army Commander-in-Chief General of the Army Javier Iturriaga del Campo, who delivered a message of recognition to the team. The group will travel to Antarctica in mid-November 2025 to operate the Army Antarctic Base (BAE) 'Capitán General Bernardo O'Higgins Riquelme', one of Chile's most southern and strategic installations, established in 1948. The commander of the deployment, Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Torres B., emphasized the significant responsibility of leading a mission in such a remote environment, stating the team will support scientific activities, protect the environment, comply with the Antarctic Treaty and international agreements, and uphold these commitments through daily operations. A key focus will be the implementation of a new Environmental Management System (SGA) aligned with ISO 14001 standards, developed through collaboration between the Army's Environmental Department, the Antarctic Affairs Center, and previous base personnel. This system will standardize processes for activity records, environmental impact assessments, waste control, and environmental monitoring, with specialized personnel such as Veterinary Nurse Sergeant 1st Daniel González F., the first designated environmental officer at the base, leading implementation. Logistically, the team must maintain essential systems—including workshops, generators, warehouses, and communication networks—to ensure base autonomy during winter months when external support is impossible. The mission also includes surveillance patrols and rescue operations conducted by the O'Higgins Search and Rescue Section (SERO), trained for extreme conditions. Scientifically, the base will continue supporting the Chilean Antarctic Institute (INACH) and Chilean and international universities in research on climate change, marine and terrestrial ecosystems.

title: Течение вокруг Антарктиды ослабло в 3 раза: что с ним случилось
content: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC), a massive flow of cold water encircling Antarctica and connecting the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans, has weakened by a factor of three compared to the previous interglacial period around 130,000 years ago, according to a study published on October 9, 2025. Scientists aboard the research vessel JOIDES Resolution, led by Dr. Michael Weber from the University of Bonn's Institute of Geosciences, extracted sediment cores from depths of 3,000 to 4,000 meters in the Scotia Sea. By analyzing particle size distribution—specifically particles between 0.1 and 0.063 millimeters—they reconstructed historical changes in current speed, as faster currents transport finer particles, which settle only when the flow slows. The data revealed that ACC velocity was three times higher during the last interglacial period than in recent millennia, despite similar global temperatures. This unexpected finding is attributed to the Milankovitch cycles: a simultaneous peak in Earth's orbital eccentricity (every ~100,000 years) and axial tilt/precession (every ~21,000 years) during the last warm period, which intensified westerly winds driving the ACC. The study also found the ACC shifted poleward by at least five degrees of latitude (approximately 600 km) during the last interglacial, bringing warmer waters closer to the Antarctic ice sheets and contributing to a sea level rise of 6–9 meters. Researchers, including project lead Xufeng Zheng from Hainan University, emphasize that future studies must integrate geological records with climate modeling to understand how natural cycles interact with anthropogenic climate change, which is critical for accurately predicting future oceanic and climatic shifts.

title: It's Antarctica or Planetary Collapse
content: The Medium.com article reports unprecedented heat and ice loss in East Antarctica. In March 2022, temperatures at Concordia Station spiked 39 °C (70 °F) above normal, raising the typical -54 °C to an almost comfortable -15 °C. Within the same week, warm rain fell where only blizzards should, and the Conger Ice Shelf collapsed into the ocean. In 2023, Antarctic sea ice fell 10 % below the already low 2022 extent; by July 15 % of the ice was gone—an area larger than Argentina—and by September the ice reached its lowest maximum ever, a "five-sigma event". On July 30 2024, ground temperatures surged 28 °C (over 50 °F) above normal, and the South Pole logged its warmest July in decades, 6.2 °C (11 °F) above normal. The article describes these events as unprecedented and suggests they may signal planetary collapse.
